perspective:
Harold Padilla’s available information:

- Harold knows he is a project manager. He knows Arthur Begum as a police officer and friend/advisor he trusts.
- He felt frustrated and anxious because he believed his project team was unmotivated and affecting progress. He arranged and attended a coffee-shop meeting with Arthur.
- He told Arthur his team seemed unmotivated and that he was at his wit’s end. He heard Arthur advise understanding what drives each team member individually, having one-on-one conversations, and making people feel valued/understood personally.
- After that talk, Harold felt hopeful and relieved. He decided to implement Arthur’s advice in team meetings.
- Harold told the team he wanted one-on-one chats to understand their motivations. He heard Team Member 1 say it could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they were open to it. Harold said he would schedule time and wanted the project to succeed together.
- Later, Harold noticed/believed the team still was not responding well. He felt disappointed and worried and discussed alternative strategies with Arthur.
- He heard Arthur say there might be deeper issues: personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and that Harold might need to dig deeper.
- Harold decided to investigate team dynamics more deeply. In one-on-one meetings, he told team members he noticed performance issues and asked for concerns.
- He heard Team Member 1 say there was tension among a few team members affecting work. He heard Team Member 2 say they felt overwhelmed by workload and stressed, making motivation hard.
- Harold said he would look into resolving conflicts and see about redistributing tasks to ease pressure, telling them their well-being mattered.
- Harold felt optimistic and empowered. He decided to create a more supportive, open team environment. He announced regular feedback sessions and team-building activities.
- He heard Team Member 1 say that sounded great and would help; Team Member 2 agreed it was good their concerns were being addressed. Harold said their input and well-being were crucial to success.

He does not have access to any private thoughts, hidden motives, or narrator-only information about Arthur or the team beyond what they said or did in his presence.
